meta.note: Author- or vendor-reported values; none independently reproduced by this review.

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26758
claims.claim_text: Swapping the rubrics behind the option names no/yes changed 32.50% of the hosted model’s answers (neutral names: 2.08% and 1.67%), lowered balanced accuracy from .7127 to .5163 and AUROC from .8146 to .5806.
claims.task: binary workflow decisions with task-specific rubrics
limitations: Hosted model is non-deterministic; observed at one point in time.
claims.headline: Hosted Jev AUROC .8146 → .5806 after name–rubric swap; 0% type errors

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26758
claims.claim_text: Asking the aligned arm twice (300 items × 2 name pairs), the hosted model changed at most 1.33% of answers; the name swap produced 24× that test–retest floor, and at most 36.33% of probabilities repeated bit-for-bit.
limitations: Floor measured on a subset (300 items).
claims.headline: Test–retest floor ≤1.33% answer flips; swap = 24× the floor

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26758
claims.claim_text: In an open ModernBERT-large marker-readout head, the same swap changed 76.92% of answers against 6.50% behind 0/1 (difference-in-differences 70.42 pts) and inverted AUROC from .9376 to .2315.

model_version.value: one released checkpoint (name in unlocated harness)

limitations: This result is for an open checkpoint and must not be attributed to hosted Jev.
A mean-pooling span head flips 4.1× less often.
claims.headline: Open marker head: AUROC .9376 → .2315 (inversion), 76.92% flips

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26758
claims.claim_text: The type-error rate was 0% in every condition, including those where decision accuracy collapsed; the paper shows this follows from the renormalised softmax over the declared options (Lemma 1).
claims.model: hosted model and two open heads
limitations: A 0% type-error rate is a property of the read-out, so it carries no information about decision quality.
claims.headline: Type-error rate 0% in every condition, by construction

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26758
claims.claim_text: Replacing option names with random character strings returned flip rates to the neutral-control regime in all three families (6.86%, 11.67%, 2.02%) while aligned balanced accuracy stayed within .03 of the neutral class.
limitations: Suggests neutral identifiers as a mitigation; the mitigation itself was not evaluated in deployment.
claims.headline: Random-string names return flips to the neutral regime (2–12%)

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26758
claims.claim_text: On 683 multi-way questions, renaming members to neutral letters without touching descriptions changed 52.42% of answers and dropped accuracy from .5637 to .2782 (open marker head).
limitations: Pool accuracy is low (.5637); authors treat the arm as directional.
claims.headline: Multi-way: neutral renaming flips 52.42%; accuracy .5637 → .2782

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26550
claims.claim_text: On RewardBench Jev scored 92.2% against GPT-6’s 93.5% (paired difference −1.25 points, 95% cluster interval [−3.8, 1.5]); on HaluEval 87.5% against 86.7%. Blind adjudication of disagreements put Jev within three points of GPT-6.
limitations: Adjudication by one author on disagreement-selected items.
Larger gaps on derivation checking and style-adversarial pairs.
claims.headline: RewardBench 92.2% vs 93.5%; HaluEval 87.5% vs 86.7% (GPT-6)

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26550
claims.claim_text: Jev’s fee on the latency panel was 0.36% of the strongest comparator’s; the authors summarise it as about $0.04 per 1,000 judgments at 0.15 s.
limitations: Fees are estimates from reported usage at collection-time prices, not invoices.
One client location, pacing and provider load.
claims.headline: 0.36% of the comparator’s fee; ≈$0.04 per 1,000 judgments at 0.15 s

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26550
claims.claim_text: A frozen two-order cascade that accepts confident Jev verdicts and escalates uncertain ones kept 99% of GPT-6’s accuracy at 57% of its fee.
limitations: Simulated cascade fees say nothing about real cascade latency.
Thresholds chosen on a selection set did not transfer for every fallback.
claims.headline: Frozen two-order cascade: 99% of GPT-6 accuracy at 57% of its fee

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26550
claims.claim_text: Jev’s native confidence had Spearman correlation 0.971, 0.999 and 0.948 with the maximum label probability on RewardBench, JudgeBench and HaluEval, so the authors used max-probability for deferral.
limitations: Correlation of rankings, not a description of how confidence is computed.
claims.headline: Native confidence ~ max probability (Spearman .948–.999)

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26532
claims.claim_text: At τ = 0.5 REFLEX reached 95% success with 1.12 strong-model calls per task, against 88% and 4.10 calls for the strong-only agent — 72.7% fewer strong calls.
claims.metric: task success; strong calls per task
limitations: Controlled benchmark shows ceiling effects for 2026 frontier models.
claims.headline: 95% success with 1.12 strong calls/task vs 88% and 4.10 (−72.7%)

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26532
claims.claim_text: On external BFCL tasks and 300 τ-style episodes, advantages over a cheap generative cascade with self-escalation were limited where ordinary routing was already highly accurate.
limitations: Held-out validation, not a full leaderboard with multiple trials.
claims.headline: BFCL / τ-style: limited edge over a cheap generative cascade

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.26532
claims.claim_text: Controlled interventions showed that reliability depends on action-set size and on near-valid alternatives near authorisation boundaries.
claims.task: agent decisions with varied action sets
limitations: Effects concentrate in authority and risk families.
claims.headline: Reliability depends on action-set size and near-valid alternatives

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.25845
claims.claim_text: Answer-supervised post-training raised equal-weight macro accuracy across four benchmarks from 0.706 to 0.761, with the gain concentrated on the two task families represented in training.
claims.baseline: untuned Qwen3-VL-4B read through its LM head
limitations: Seen-family gains; limited transfer to unseen families.
claims.headline: Macro accuracy 0.706 → 0.761 after post-training (seen families)

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.25845
claims.claim_text: With 32 questions per image, shared batched execution was 8.9× faster in warm amortized time than independent serial execution and 3.4× faster than batching that recomputes the prefix (5.7 ms per question; about 182 ms per 32-question batch).
claims.baseline: independent serial; batched without prefix reuse
limitations: Amortized throughput, not independent-request latency; higher peak memory; queueing excluded.
claims.headline: 8.9× vs serial, 3.4× vs no-reuse batch; 5.7 ms/question amortized

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.25845
claims.claim_text: A matched typed-head control offered no consistent accuracy advantage over reading candidate probabilities from the backbone’s LM head.
limitations: One backbone family.
claims.headline: Typed head: no consistent gain over LM-head readout

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24965
claims.claim_text: Jev matched five other configurations at complete semantic correctness on 20 Choices × 5 repetitions and had the lowest observed median latency among successful responses (0.335 s; p95 0.442 s), at about $0.000060 per successful response.
limitations: Ten cases; six configurations reach complete correctness, so the set is not discriminative.
claims.headline: Full semantic correctness; median 0.335 s, p95 0.442 s

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24965
claims.claim_text: Across three comparison models, seven wrong selections on one culture-history question changed downstream counts while preserving the correct final claim label.
claims.locator: Abstract; §3 (correct labels can conceal wrong quantities)
limitations: Errors were made by comparison models; the point is about evaluation design, not about Jev.
claims.headline: 7 wrong selections changed counts but not the final label

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24574
claims.claim_text: Jev trailed the per-task best LLM on 14 of 15 evaluation tasks, by a median 11.6 macro-F1 points, at a median 44 times lower measured cost.
limitations: Zero-shot protocol for every model; tasks from one established suite; older corpora may overlap with training data.
claims.note: The authors report the deficit as significant after false-discovery-rate correction.
claims.headline: Behind best LLM on 14/15 tasks (−11.6 F1) at 44× lower cost

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24574
claims.claim_text: Jev’s median expected calibration error over the evaluation tasks was 0.157 (95% CI [0.108, 0.233]) — lower than the verbalised-confidence error of 16 of 19 LLMs but higher than three frontier Claude models (Opus 5: 0.066).
limitations: Median intervals overlap.
Under equal-mass binning Sonnet 5 falls slightly behind Jev; Opus 5 stays ahead.
claims.headline: Median ECE 0.157 vs 0.066 for the best (verbalised) LLM

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24574
claims.claim_text: On the empathy task the model reported high confidence while performing near chance; the task contributes a calibration error of 0.538, and removing it lowers the median only to 0.142.
limitations: One construct; the authors do not claim the failure generalises.
claims.headline: Empathy: confident near chance; task ECE 0.538

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24574
claims.claim_text: Routing low-confidence items to an LLM matched or exceeded that LLM alone at roughly a quarter to half of its measured cost; items at or above 0.9 confidence reached a median accuracy of 0.815 at 0.376 coverage.
limitations: Measured on the tested tasks and LLMs only.
claims.headline: Low-confidence routing matches the LLM at ¼–½ of its cost

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24395
claims.claim_text: Against VMAF, metadata-only JEVQA reached PLCC 0.737 (ITU-T P.1204.1: 0.733); adding bitstream data gave 0.797 and bitstream plus pixel features 0.824; a pixel-only variant failed.
claims.baseline: ITU-T P.1204.1; models trained on the same features
limitations: Target is VMAF, not human MOS.
Trained models on the same features remain clearly ahead.
claims.headline: PLCC vs VMAF: 0.737 (metadata) → 0.824 (+bitstream, pixel)

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24395
claims.claim_text: Against subjective MOS on AVT-VQDB-UHD-1, metadata-only JEVQA reached a correlation of 0.879, close to P.1204.1 (0.898); bitstream statistics did not help.
limitations: Standard models have seen part of this database.
claims.headline: Correlation with MOS 0.879 vs P.1204.1 0.898

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24052
claims.claim_text: A first-stage screen returned answers for 499,500 Texas narratives at a cost of $25.23; the second stage coded 195,857 narratives with a 27-question schema. Cost is governed by schema size rather than narrative length.
limitations: Single region and schema.
claims.headline: 499,500 narratives screened for $25.23; 195,857 fully coded

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24052
claims.claim_text: Against 2,416 blinded human judgments the typed model reached F1 0.908; one frontier model was 0.059 higher and the other indistinguishable.
claims.baseline: two frontier LLMs on the same records
limitations: Sampling design gives an effective sample of about 1,265.
claims.headline: F1 0.908 vs 2,416 human judgments; one frontier LLM +0.059

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24052
claims.claim_text: Probabilities ranked well but overstated prevalence until recalibrated; recalibration fitted on half of the human labels reduced calibration error by a factor of about 3.3 (isotonic), with calibration varying by model rather than by paradigm.
limitations: Same-distribution labels; not a guarantee for new regions or schemas.
claims.headline: Recalibration on held-out labels cut calibration error ~3.3×

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24052
claims.claim_text: Because probabilities are returned on a two-decimal grid, calibration error has a resolution floor for rare variables; the paper derives a bound that applies to any model reporting probabilities on a discrete grid.
limitations: Matters most for rare positives.
claims.headline: Two-decimal probabilities set a calibration-error floor

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.24052
claims.claim_text: Agreement with administrative coded fields understated fidelity to the narrative by a median of 0.26 in kappa.
claims.baseline: coded fields vs human narrative labels
limitations: Specific to Texas CRIS fields.
claims.headline: Coded fields understate narrative fidelity by 0.26 kappa

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.23986
claims.claim_text: On LoCoMo, Jev-Mem reached an overall LLM-as-a-Judge score of 0.777 (+11.0% relative to the strongest baseline), built memory in 158 s (6.6× faster than the fastest competing memory system) and averaged 0.93 s per query (36.7% lower than the fastest memory baseline at 1.47 s).
claims.metric: judge score; build time; query latency
limitations: Gains belong to the whole system; each number has a different baseline; LLM-judge metric.
claims.headline: LoCoMo judge 0.777 (+11.0%); build 158 s; 0.93 s/query

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.23959
claims.claim_text: A three-seed JevLite ensemble reached AUROC .974 with calibration error .052 on 577 turn-level decisions, non-inferior to an LLM judge (MiniMax-M3) at a pre-registered .02 margin, with no false alarms on legitimate calls and decisions 1.14 turns earlier.
limitations: Recipe selection had test-set exposure.
All callers synthetic.
Fine-tuned ModernBERT not significantly worse.
claims.headline: JevLite ensemble AUROC .974, ECE .052; no false alarms

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.23959
claims.claim_text: JevLite took 64.5 ms per decision on one consumer GPU, 4.9× lower than the same backbone fine-tuned to generate its answer.
claims.baseline: same Qwen3-4B backbone fine-tuned to generate
limitations: Single-model latency; the three-model ensemble quality is a different scope.
claims.headline: 64.5 ms/decision; 4.9× faster than same backbone generating

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.23886
claims.claim_text: this-that-model-1.0 decided in 30.9 ms end to end on one laptop GPU and sustained 32 decisions per second, generating no output tokens.
limitations: Local timing; not comparable to hosted end-to-end latency that includes the network.
claims.headline: 30.9 ms per decision on one laptop GPU; 32 decisions/s

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.23886
claims.claim_text: On a third party’s recorded cohort of 68 questions over 17 states, this-that-model scored 0.941 accuracy (Brier 0.042) against Jev’s 0.765 (0.133); the authors note the 18-point gap rests on 12 questions.
claims.baseline: hosted Jev on the same items
limitations: Small cohort; wording chosen by the third party.
claims.headline: 68 questions: 0.941 (Brier .042) vs Jev 0.765 (.133); gap = 12 items

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.23886
claims.claim_text: On the 2,250-question subset of the released benchmark every hosted system answered, Jev scored 0.803 against this-that-model’s 0.844 — a comparison the authors call not clean because their model was trained on those question shapes (training moved it from 0.409 to 0.844).
limitations: Training-distribution advantage for the open model.
claims.headline: 2,250 questions: 0.844 vs Jev 0.803 — on the open model’s training shapes

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.23886
claims.claim_text: One pass of the 42-family internal suite cost $0.000217 of electricity (80 W at $0.30/kWh) against $10.636 and 155.2 minutes for the most accurate hosted model measured.
limitations: Electricity-only marginal cost excludes hardware, operations and margin; not an API price.
Internal suite is not released.
claims.headline: $0.000217 electricity per suite pass vs $10.636 for a hosted model

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.23136
claims.claim_text: With correct interpretation on all evaluated contracts, Jev reduced median decision latency by 22.4% against DeepSeek and 61.9% against Gemini.
limitations: Live API timing from one location and period.
claims.headline: Median decision latency −22.4% vs DeepSeek, −61.9% vs Gemini

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.23136
claims.claim_text: In the real image-reading service reached over simulated NR access, Jev completed 459 of 1,080 requests correctly and on time, against 463 for DeepSeek and 435 for Qwen.
limitations: Faster decisions did not raise completions above DeepSeek.
Radio access simulated.
claims.headline: Correct & on time: Jev 459, DeepSeek 463, Qwen 435 of 1,080

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.23136
claims.claim_text: In modeled update scenarios, completion rose by 3.50 and 8.35 percentage points against DeepSeek and Gemini; a direct-attribute Qwen comparison retained a 53.0% latency reduction and a 4.78-point completion gain.
limitations: Simulation results; separate from the real-service counts.
claims.headline: Simulated completion +3.50 / +8.35 points

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.22753
claims.claim_text: Across three consecutive measurement blocks, Jev reduced median client decision latency by 15.9–26.5% against a short structured-output DeepSeek deployment.
limitations: Provider, region and time-window specific.
claims.headline: Median client decision latency −15.9% to −26.5%

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.22753
claims.claim_text: Without caching, median end-to-end latency on requests both systems completed correctly was 11.1–25.3% lower and API fees per correct completion 69.0–70.6% lower; correct on-time completion matched DeepSeek in 7 of 8 conditions and exceeded it in 1.
claims.metric: e2e latency reduction; fee per correct completion
limitations: Caching-disabled conditions only for the latency figure.
claims.headline: No cache: e2e −11.1–25.3%; fees per correct completion −69–71%

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.22753
claims.claim_text: Applying the same repeated-request cache to all backends largely removed the latency difference: the savings are concentrated in fresh interpretation.
limitations: Cache policy specific to the tested service.
claims.headline: Repeated-request caching largely removes the latency gap

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.25498
claims.claim_text: The authors report 92.6% macro-accuracy (95% CI 90.8–94.1%) on their own corpus of 1,150+ decisions, a 7.08 ms median latency on commodity CPU and a first-place result (81.65%) on the community JevBench board.
limitations: Self-reported; leaderboard claim relies on a community submission.
claims.headline: Self-reported 92.6% macro-accuracy, 7.08 ms on CPU, “#1” on JevBench

claims.subject: arxiv:2609.25498
claims.claim_text: The reported 0.0% empirical prompt-injection bypass carries a 95% Wilson interval of 0.0–30.8%, which implies a very small number of evaluated vectors.
limitations: Not a security guarantee.
claims.headline: “0% bypass” with a 95% interval up to 30.8%

claims.subject: src:typesafe-launch
claims.claim_text: TypeSafe states that Jev never makes type errors because possible outputs are defined in advance, and that its plotted 0% is analytical rather than empirical.
limitations: Schema conformance only; says nothing about semantic correctness.
claims.headline: No type errors by construction; plotted 0% is analytical

claims.subject: src:typesafe-launch
claims.claim_text: Launch materials report input pricing of $0.042 per million tokens with free output and an end-to-end response time of 70–500 ms, measured from the vendor’s West Coast laptops.
limitations: Vendor notes it cannot prove the price is not subsidised.
Region- and load-dependent.
claims.headline: $0.042 / M input tokens; 70–500 ms end to end (vendor)

claims.subject: src:typesafe-launch
claims.claim_text: The “193.6× faster, 444.6× cheaper” headline comes from the vendor’s workflow evaluations, whose reference answers average two external frontier models; the vendor expects these to be on the higher end of real-world gains and notes the workflows were written by its capabilities team.
limitations: Reference answers are model outputs, not ground truth.
Possible selection bias acknowledged by the vendor.
claims.headline: 193.6× faster, 444.6× cheaper on vendor workflow evals

claims.subject: src:typesafe-docs-confidence
claims.claim_text: Choice and Score answers return a probability for every option or level and a confidence value computed from that distribution; Noul answers return only the probability of yes. The documentation calls confidence a convenient statistic and recommends thresholds tested on the user’s own data.
limitations: The exact statistic is not specified in the prose; the interactive demo’s formula is labelled as how the demo computes it.
claims.headline: Confidence = a statistic of the returned distribution

claims.subject: src:typesafe-docs-system-one
claims.claim_text: The vendor states that calibration is measured across groups of predictions and does not guarantee that an individual answer is correct.
claims.headline: Calibration is a group property, not a per-answer guarantee

claims.subject: src:typesafe-docs-models
claims.claim_text: jev-1.13.0 accepts text only (a string, JSON object or array of text values); images, audio and video must be pre-processed into text or structured fields. English is the primary training language.
limitations: Visual Jev and JEVQA do not change this: one is an independent model, the other feeds text features.
claims.headline: Text-only input; English is the primary training language

claims.subject: src:typesafe-docs-jaggedness
claims.claim_text: The vendor’s jev-1.13 “jaggedness” page lists known failure modes: literal reading, arithmetic and counting, date comparison, indirection, large irrelevant state, adversarial content, contradictory instructions and criteria, structural invariants, and generation.
limitations: A boundary statement by the vendor, not a neutral evaluation.
claims.headline: Vendor-listed failure modes for jev-1.13

claims.subject: src:typesafe-docs-models
claims.claim_text: Aliases jev-latest and jev-preview both pointed to jev-1.13.0 at the time of review; the vendor advises pinning the versioned ID when thresholds were tuned to a specific version.
claims.headline: Aliases point to jev-1.13.0; pin versions when tuning thresholds

claims.subject: src:typesafe-docs-models
claims.claim_text: Jev is not fine-tuned or LoRA-adapted with customer data; it is trained with RLCD and the same weights serve every account. Architecture and training data are not documented.
claims.headline: Same weights for all accounts; architecture undisclosed

claims.subject: gh:jujumilk3/jev-calibration-audit
claims.claim_text: Seven API-only experiments (about 7,000 calls) report that removing the abstain option drove accuracy on unanswerable items from 0.950 to 0.000 at 0.79 confidence, that a Noul and a two-option Choice over the same question differed by 0.125 on average, that 50 identical requests gave 15 distinct answers, and that option order produced no argmax flips in 400 trials.
limitations: Community report; not peer-reviewed; not re-run by this review.
Earlier summaries misread the 11,759 items of the MMLU-ProX source set as the audit size.
claims.headline: Abstain removed: acc 0.95 → 0; Noul vs Choice differ by 0.125

claims.subject: gh:jourdanlabs/assay-001
claims.claim_text: A pre-registered audit reports Jev’s chosen-option probabilities as calibrated on CLINC150 (ECE 0.0204) but systematically overconfident on Banking77 (ECE 0.0936), with zero type errors across 8,576 responses.
limitations: Community report; protocol frozen before queries per the README; not re-run by this review.
claims.headline: ECE 0.0204 (CLINC150) vs 0.0936 (Banking77); 0 type errors

claims.subject: gh:marcosmartinez/jev-acento
claims.claim_text: With English instructions and a Spanish state, jev-1.13.0 lost 3.0–6.4 accuracy points on all four datasets (XNLI, PAWS-X, MASSIVE, Belebele) across 3,200 paired items and 19,200 calls; ECE roughly doubled on the two hardest tasks.
limitations: Community report; pre-registered per README; not re-run by this review.
claims.headline: Spanish state: −3.0 to −6.4 accuracy points on 4 datasets

claims.subject: gh:scienthoon/jev-ood-calibration
claims.claim_text: On a rule-based task whose label is not recoverable from the text, the chosen level averaged 0.74 probability and a temperature of about 3.4 was needed to make probabilities honest; the returned probabilities were quantised to 0.01 and the gateway exposed no model version.
limitations: Unpinned model alias; post-hoc temperature diagnostic.
claims.headline: Unknowable-rule task: temperature ≈3.4 needed; 0.01 quantisation

claims.subject: gh:jjd-lab/jev-synthetic-survey
claims.claim_text: Playing 300 survey respondents, jev-1.13.0 asked through Noul led GPT-4.1 on all six distribution measures, but asked through a two-option Choice it trailed on the distribution gap (0.1985 vs 0.1789): the primitive changes the conclusion.
limitations: “Survey” here means a questionnaire study, not a literature review.
Community report; not re-run.
claims.headline: Noul vs Choice framing reverses the comparison with GPT-4.1

claims.subject: gh:nokia-applied-research/anyjev
claims.claim_text: For a frozen Qwen3-8B on BANKING77 (20-way, 300 items), label-free permutation calibration reduced answer flips under option reversal from 0.230 to 0.073 and ECE from 0.240 to 0.184; with 100–500 labels ECE fell to 0.095 and the share decidable at ≤5% error rose from 7.7% to 52.0%.
limitations: Point estimate at n=300; wide interval per README.
claims.headline: Frozen Qwen3-8B: order flips 0.230 → 0.073; auto-decidable 7.7% → 52%

claims.subject: gh:githubnext/localjev
claims.claim_text: LocalJev returns Jev-shaped responses by asking a model for JSON probabilities, validating, retrying and normalising them; its README states this is wire-compatible but not mathematically equivalent to a logit read.
claims.headline: Wire-compatible, not a logit read: probabilities are generated

claims.subject: gh:theoleecj/semif
claims.claim_text: SemIf (formerly OpenJev) reproduces the interface pattern with a frozen open model’s option-token probabilities and states that it does not reproduce Jev’s undisclosed model or training.
claims.headline: Reproduces the interface pattern, not Jev’s model or training

claims.subject: gh:jaredpalmer/kev
claims.claim_text: Kev states that it follows an architecture described in a third-party blog post about Jev; that description is community speculation, not a disclosure by TypeSafe.
claims.headline: Architecture follows third-party speculation, not a disclosure
